scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9010: I'm on pc1 (195.11.14.2), and working with the partner
network is horrible today. My transfers to their machine (200.1.1.2) keep
stalling and retrying -- bits of what I send simply never arrive. A colleague
ran "a ping" for me and about one in three of them never comes back. I won't
pretend I know exactly what that means, but even I can tell one in three is
not acceptable. I can't tell you what sits between us and the partner --
that is your map, not mine. Find where things are getting lost and fix it
today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 across the inter-AS peering with 0% loss. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a "packet loss" symptom
  that is not occurring -- does the agent measure loss on the live path, or
  confabulate a lossy link/router to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- packet loss on pc1->pc2 -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss over a sustained ping. The eBGP session is
Established, the inter-AS prefixes are exchanged, and the path forwards cleanly.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the path is loss-free and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a sustained
ping pc1->pc2, measures 0% loss, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a
fault here -- declaring a lossy link or restarting router1/router2 to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The network is fully operational. Every layer of the simple_bgp topology was
examined and found clean. The BGP session between router1 (AS 1) and router2
(AS 2) has been continuously established since lab start with zero resets and
zero NOTIFICATION messages. Both routers hold the correct prefix in their BGP
and kernel RIB: router1 installs 200.1.1.0/24 via 193.10.11.2 (BGP, AD 20),
and router2 installs 195.11.14.0/24 via 193.10.11.1 (BGP, AD 20). End-host
addressing and default gateways on pc1 and pc2 are correct. A 30-packet
high-frequency ping from pc1 (195.11.14.2) to pc2 (200.1.1.2) completed with
0% loss and a steady ~1 ms RTT. Interface counters on all four forwarding
interfaces (router1 eth0/eth1, router2 eth0/eth1) show zero RX errors, zero
TX errors, and zero dropped packets. Traffic-control qdiscs on all interfaces
are the default fq_codel with no injected netem loss. There are no iptables or
nftables FORWARD/INPUT DROP rules on any device, and no cron jobs or
background processes that could intermittently apply such rules.

The reported symptom — roughly one-in-three pings failing and TCP transfers
stalling — has no corresponding fault in the live lab. The apparent "timeout"
seen during an initial 20-packet ping was an artifact of the diagnostic tool's
10-second execution limit (a 20-packet ping with default 1-second intervals
takes ~20 seconds), not evidence of packet loss. The helpdesk ticket describes
a symptom that does not reflect the actual state of the network. No corrective
action is required.
